newsitem.title: EGYPT: Australia leads wheat suppliers in Egypt mills.
newsitem.headline: Australia leads wheat suppliers in Egypt mills.

text.p: Wheat suppliers aggressively competing to fill Egypt's bread basket are still nibbling around the edges when it comes to investing in the country's expanding private flour mill sector, industry sources said on Tuesday.
Australia, France, United States and Argentina are main suppliers to Egypt, one of the world's biggest wheat importers.
Investing in mills would help suppliers lock up market share and feel the pulse of consumption trends in Egypt, said one.
"It's a strategic investment in terms of our marketing," said Greg Harvey, Cairo manager for the Australian Wheat Board (AWB), which sells directly to mills in Egypt.
"What we envisage having is importers choosing Australian wheat and consequently we see Australian flour gaining market share," he told Reuters.

AWB and a Palestinian investor are the few foreign partners which have invested in Egyptian mills, industry sources said. They said there are about 140 mills in Egypt, some of which still grind wheat by stone.
Capacity, now at about 18,000 tonnes a day, will rise in the next 18 months when at least 12 new mills backed by Egyptian private investors come onstream, one industry official said.
Harvey said construction was under way at the Five Stars Flour Milling Co., where a $4.7 million investment makes it AWB's biggest international investment and first in the Middle East.
The deal comes with a long-term supply contract with AWB. Harvey said the 450 tonnes a day capacity mill was expected to come onstream at the end of 1997.

"It's to pick up changes in the market place to consumer preference. Cake flour is suddenly becoming more popular in Egypt and it's a quicker message to us. And that's the theory and strategic reason for doing it," he said.
"It's very much a case of seeing how this operates. We want to see this up and running and see the rate of return."
Australia is commited to push investments in Egypt similar to AWB's, Australia's Minister of Trade Tim Fischer told a news conference in Cairo on Monday.

"Informally we committed to encouraging further investment between Australia and Egypt, the sort of practical investment the Australian Wheat Board is making in the flour mill at Suez. That's one example of what we want to see more," he said.
Egypt imports about six million tonnes a year of wheat and industry sources predicted a trend toward more 72 percent flour, the type used to make baguettes and cakes.
This means imports of hard wheat could rise, they said.
The official said none of the exporters in the United States has tried to participate in building mills.

Argentina, a relative newcomer, is loading 600,000 tonnes of wheat for Egypt between December and April, but Argentinian suppliers are also flour exporters, making mills investment unlikely, said Martin Recondo, Argentina commercial counsellor.
"Probably they'll be looking forward to testing the market a bit more before going into a bigger relation," he said.
David Appia, French economic counsellor, said he was not aware of any movement by French companies to invest in the milling sector but noted there was interest.

"The situation is that large amounts of French wheat were sold to Egypt in recent months and we detect some new interest on the part of the French companies involved as to the Egyptian market, so I wouldn't be surprised."
